title: Rabbi Judah and the calf
hookLine: the Talmud records its heroes' flaws and quarrels
carry: the talmud keeps its heroes' flaws, and their turning
last: A JOKE FIRST, THEN LEARNING IN AWE.

lines: A CALF RUNS TO THE RABBI.
GO. FOR THIS YOU WERE CREATED.
THE TALMUD TELLS IT ON PURPOSE.
cards: A calf is being led to slaughter. It breaks away, runs to a great rabbi, and hides its head in the folds of his robe, crying. The rabbi is Rabbi Judah the Prince, the sage tradition credits with editing the Mishnah.
He looks down at the frightened animal and says: go. For this you were created. And he lets them take it away.
The Talmud tells this about one of its own heroes, plainly, and it doesn't stop there.

teach.b: Tractate Bava Metzia tells it plainly. Because he showed no compassion, suffering came upon Rabbi Judah, and stayed with him for years.

Then one day his maid was sweeping the house and came upon some young weasels, and began to sweep them out. He stopped her. Let them be, he said, and quoted the Psalm: "His tender mercies are over all His works."
And the Talmud says that because he showed compassion, the suffering left him. Notice what the book has done. It could have polished him into a statue.

teach.h: A GIANT IN A COLD MOMENT.
teach.b: Instead it shows a giant in a cold moment, the cost of that moment, and the small act that turned him. And it isn't a lone story.
The Talmud also tells how Rabban Gamliel, the head of the sages, was removed from leadership after he publicly shamed a colleague.

teach.h: HEROES WHO FAIL ON THE PAGE.
teach.b: The heroes misjudge, wound each other and change, right there on the page, in front of every student who will ever open it. Why would a tradition tell its children that their heroes failed?
One answer: if the sages were perfect, nobody could follow them. A flawless teacher leaves you nothing to do but admire.

teach.h: A TEACHER WHO TURNED LEAVES A PATH.
teach.b: A teacher who failed and turned leaves you a path. And the teaching keeps going past the teacher's flaw. Rabbi Judah's Mishnah is still studied, and so is the story of the calf and the weasels, side by side.

how: Students of the Talmud meet its sages' mistakes and quarrels in the text itself, and teachers often discuss what those stories teach about humility, compassion and repair.

games.q: what does “the sages were human” mean?
o: the sages were judged by courts like anyone
the rabbis claimed no special learning at all

it tells them on purpose, like Rabbi Judah and the calf.
Rabbi Judah's suffering left after he spared the young weasels
he said let them be, and quoted Psalm 145:9.

games.q: you're Rabbi Judah's maid, sweeping the house, and you find young weasels. you start to sweep them out. what does he say?
o: let them be: His tender mercies are over all His works.
call someone else to deal with them.
games.why: he stops her and quotes the Psalm. the Talmud says that because he showed compassion, his suffering left him.

practice: Bring to mind someone you look up to, and let one of their real flaws come into view. Don't defend them, and don't throw them away; hold both at once, what you admire and where they fell short.
Then, gently, let one of your own flaws stand beside theirs.

wordCard.voice: The sages were human. The Talmud keeps its heroes' cold moments, quarrels and turnings on the page, so students can follow them, not only admire them. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: sages, the wise ones; a usual word for the teachers of the Mishnah and Talmud.

carryVoice: Your line: the Talmud keeps its heroes' flaws, and their turning. Rabbi Judah turned from the calf to the weasels: his tender mercies are over all his works. Until tomorrow.
